source.title: Analysis and Optimization of Convolutional Neural Network Architectures

record.file_problem: none; full thesis text is present
record.tranche_reason: The study reports its own CIFAR-100 batch-size sweep and network-width comparisons with test accuracy outcomes, using its own CNN training setup.
record.gate_note: The batch-size sweep and width comparisons report test accuracy outcomes. Other potentially relevant material, such as dropout and optimizer discussion, is background or does not report a comparative generalization result.
record.test_reason: The study reports batch-size effects under early stopping with different training durations, not V5's fixed epoch budget. Its width comparisons do not establish widening beyond zero training error, as V2 requires. No other version receives a direct test.
record.authors_conclusion: The record accurately paraphrases the author's conclusion: smaller batches improved accuracy empirically, but batches can also be too small. This conclusion concerns the early-stopped recipe and does not establish the fixed-epoch claim.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses its own CIFAR-100 CNN baseline and batch-size sweep, with Adam, data augmentation, early stopping, and other stated setup choices; it does not reproduce the referenced batch-size studies' recipes.
record.method_sensitivity: Batch size changes test accuracy; batch size 8 is worse than 16 and 32, while 128 is worse than 64.

fits_no_version.finding: With early stopping, CIFAR-100 single-model accuracy peaks at batches 16–32: 64.16% and 64.11%, versus 63.38% at 64, 62.23% at 128, and 61.93% at 8. Training durations vary by batch size.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: For this CNN and early-stopping recipe, intermediate batch sizes outperform both the smallest and largest tested batches.

fits_no_version.finding: Table 5.8 reports mixed test-accuracy changes after widening individual CNN layers, alongside fewer training epochs. Training error for the widened variants is unavailable.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Under this regularized CNN recipe, the accuracy benefit of widening depends on which layer is widened.

record.problems: The batch-size comparison reports accuracy on one dataset and does not provide training accuracy for each batch-size condition in Table 5.9; the reported standard deviations reflect variation across models.
record.rows_left_out: Width variants in Table 5.8 (p. 54) are not extracted because the table reports test accuracy but not training error for those conditions, so it cannot establish whether widening past zero training error changes the test error gap.

untested.parts: No paired random-label and natural-label training experiments.
No interpolation threshold or zero-training-error width is established. Width variants use regularized, early-stopped multilayer ELU CNNs.
No experimental convolutional-versus-fully-connected comparison or test of learned local connectivity.
No held-out performance comparison between adaptive optimizers and SGD.
No batch-size comparison with epochs held fixed, or controlled test of the named adaptations that remove a fixed-budget penalty.
No dropout addition, removal, or probability comparison. The regularization sweep changes L2 strength.
No magnitude-aware perturbation measure or ranking of generalization gaps.
No memorization-based removal of training examples.

record.verdict_notes: The common ceiling of 1000 epochs per training stage is not an equal realized epoch budget. Section 5.1 applies validation-based early stopping, and Table 5.9 explicitly reports differing epoch ranges. The study is not an original source for any listed version.

versions.untested_parts: No random-label training or comparison with natural labels.

The width sweep reports test accuracy but not training error for those variants, so it does not establish behavior beyond the width needed for zero training error. The networks are multi-layer CNNs with ELU, not one-hidden-layer ReLU networks.
No comparison of convolutional and fully connected networks.
No optimizer comparison of held-out performance; Adam is the baseline, and an SGD reference concerns weight updates only.
The sweep is on CIFAR-100 with the stated training setup; it does not test language models or the recipe adaptations named in the version.
Dropout is present in the baseline, but the study does not compare adding or removing dropout.
No magnitude-aware sharpness or comparison of generalization measures.
No removal of memorized training examples.

rows.subject: baseline model m
rows.note: Compared with batch sizes 16 and 32, accuracy is lower; the text says lower batch sizes generalize better, but batch size 8 does not perform best.
rows.check: Accuracy and standard deviation are correctly extracted, but batch size 8 used 81–153 epochs. The comparison does not measure V5's fixed-budget effect; lower accuracy than batches 16–32 does not qualify V5, which allows a workload-dependent threshold.

rows.subject: baseline model m
rows.note: Highest single-model accuracy in the reported batch-size sweep.
rows.check: Accuracy and standard deviation are correct. Batch size 16 used 103–173 epochs; its higher accuracy cannot establish a large-batch penalty under equal epoch budgets.

rows.subject: baseline model m
rows.note: Accuracy is close to batch size 16 and higher than batch sizes 8, 64, and 128.
rows.check: Accuracy and standard deviation are correct. Batch size 32 used 119–179 epochs. Near equality with batch size 16 is not a partial V5 effect; the required fixed-budget comparison is unavailable.

rows.check: Accuracy and standard deviation are correct. Batch size 64 used 133–195 epochs and is the recipe baseline. Its lower accuracy than batches 16–32 does not isolate V5's fixed-budget effect.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
